newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Willis lectures Costello on budget perils.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Willis lectures Costello on budget perils.

text.p: Former treasurer Ralph Willis must be having a satisfying laugh at the government, which has now had exactly the same sort of fiscal embarrassment that he suffered last year.
Today he lectured the government on the perils of budgeting.
Willis has always seemed irritated by the dishonesty of politics and keener than most politicians to tell it the way it really is.
How frustrated he must have felt last year when the new government revealed that he, of all treasurers, had presented wildly inaccurate forward estimates in his May 1995 budget.
Willis, himself an early proponent of the "underlying" budget concept, had forecast a 1996/97 budget with a small (A$590 million) underlying deficit.
Unfortunately, by March 1996 Treasury projected a 1996/97 deficit of A$7.6 billion -- the A$8 billion Beazley Black Hole we kept hearing about last year.

The fact that the budget projections were wrong should not have surprised anyone. They're always wrong. Moreover, they have consistently been wrong in the same direction (always worse, not better) since the 1990-91 recession.
Without having looked closely at all the old budget papers, Canberra Watch assumes the theme has been lower-than-forecast inflation consistently failing to deliver the expected fiscal drag.
And now the new government's projection for the very same budget has deteriorated by A$3 billion, as Treasurer Peter Costello revealed in the mid-year review last week.
So Willis today reflected on the pitfalls of forecasting during debate on the Charter of Budget Honesty Bill today:
"But all this (the Beazley Black Hole) reflected in the main was change in economic and budget parameters, some of it good change, like lower inflation.
"When these changes go against you on both sides of the ledger they can quickly make a very substantial difference to the fiscal outlook."
The Reserve Bank had noted that economic parameters had created 90 percent of the change, he noted.

"The same thing can happen with programme parameters when outlay or revenue programmes don't perform as expected, as this government has just learned with the shortfall in company tax in the current year, a shortfall of A$1.6 billion.

"And despite carpeting the treasury secretary and the commissioner for taxation in the cabinet (for these errors) the fact is that this is certain to happen again because these things are only estimates.
"They're subject to a multitude of variables and even with the most smart people in the world you'll never get it exactly right and sometimes you'll get it very wrong.
"And of course clearly in the past the economic forecasts have got it woefully wrong, as with the case with the recession in the early 90s which they never anticipated at all.
"So we should not lose sight of the fact that these outyear estimates are only broadly indicative. With each subsequent update the numbers will vary notably, sometimes very substantially."
WHILE WE'RE ON THE BUDGET
Finance Minister John Fahey was due to release the November Commonwealth Government Financial Transactions (CFT) report early in January.
But it did not appear until the afternoon of the mid-year review.
Why? Because even the previous CFT showed reason to doubt that the government would reach a A$5.6 billion 12-month underlying deficit by June, as projected in the August budget.
In October, the rolling 12-month deficit was A$13.3 billion and tending to get worse rather than better.
The November CFT that Fahey released after the review showed an A$12.3 billion 12-month deficit, still nowhere near the June target.
Clearly, the government had good reason for delaying the release -- it didn't want to let the fact of the budget's deterioration slip out early.
Next time Fahey fails to issue a CFT at a suspicious time the alarm bells should ring.
-- Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
